title: Graph Traversal — BFS & DFS
summary: BFS and DFS visit every reachable node but give fundamentally different guarantees — BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, DFS doesn't, and picking the wrong one for the job is a recurring interview slip.

slides.markdown:
Every graph algorithm you'll ever write is built on one of two exploration orders: **breadth-first search (BFS)**, which explores level by level outward from a start node, or **depth-first search (DFS)**, which commits to going as deep as possible before backtracking.

Both visit every reachable node in O(V + E) — same complexity, same reachability guarantee. What differs is the *order* they visit in, and that order carries a real guarantee BFS has and DFS doesn't: BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph. Reaching for the wrong one when "shortest" is in the problem statement is one of the most common graph mistakes in interviews.

BFS visits all of a node's direct neighbors before moving on to any of *their* neighbors — it explores in expanding "rings" outward from the start. The mechanism is a **queue**: start with the source in the queue, and repeatedly dequeue a node, enqueue its unvisited neighbors, mark them visited.

Because the queue is FIFO, nodes come out in the same order they went in — which is exactly what guarantees the level-by-level property. A node at distance 2 from the source is only ever enqueued after all distance-1 nodes are already in the queue ahead of it.

DFS picks a neighbor, commits fully to exploring everything reachable through it, and only backtracks when it hits a dead end. The mechanism is a **stack** — either the explicit call stack via recursion, or a manually managed stack for an iterative version.

Where BFS's queue enforces "finish this level before the next," DFS's stack enforces the opposite: "finish this entire branch before trying a sibling." That structural difference is the whole reason the two produce such different visiting orders on the same graph.

<<< Image: the same small tree-shaped graph shown twice side by side; left side labelled BFS shows nodes colored in concentric rings by distance from the root, with the queue's contents drawn below at one point in time; right side labelled DFS shows one long path highlighted from root to a deep leaf before backtracking, with the recursion/call stack's contents drawn below at that same point >>>

The visual should make the memory-shape difference obvious: BFS's queue at its widest holds an entire level's worth of nodes (can be O(V) wide on a bushy graph), while DFS's stack at its deepest holds one path's worth of nodes (O(depth), which can be much smaller on a wide, shallow graph).

slides.sectionTitle: Why BFS finds shortest paths and DFS doesn't
slides.markdown:
BFS's level-by-level guarantee means: the first time you reach any node, you've reached it via the shortest possible number of edges from the source. There's no way to reach a node "early" through a longer path, because every shorter path's nodes are already fully processed by the time BFS gets around to a longer one.

DFS has no such property — it might stumble onto a long, winding path to a node long before it ever considers a 2-edge shortcut to the same node, simply because that shortcut happened to be explored later in the neighbor iteration order. DFS is still correct for *reachability* (visits every node BFS would), but the *path* it finds first carries no shortest-path guarantee at all.

A natural extension: start BFS with **multiple** sources already in the queue at distance 0, instead of just one. The algorithm is otherwise unchanged — it floods outward from all starting points simultaneously, and the level-by-level guarantee still holds, now measured as "distance to the *nearest* of any source."

This is the standard approach to problems like "rotting oranges" (multiple rot sources spreading each minute) or "find the cell farthest from any water tile" — seed the queue with every source at once rather than running a separate single-source BFS per source and taking the minimum, which would be far more expensive.

| | BFS | DFS |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | Queue | Stack (explicit or call stack) |
| Memory at widest/deepest | O(width) — can be O(V) on a bushy graph | O(depth) — can be much less on a wide, shallow graph |
| Shortest path (unweighted)? | Yes, guaranteed | No guarantee |
| Natural fit | Shortest path, level-order problems, multi-source flooding | Path existence, backtracking, cycle detection, topological ordering |

Neither is strictly "better" — they answer different questions well. The interview signal is picking based on what the problem actually asks ("shortest" → BFS; "does a path exist," "all paths," "detect a cycle" → DFS), not defaulting to whichever you wrote most recently.

slides.sectionTitle: Reaching for DFS on a shortest-path problem
slides.markdown:
A problem asks for the shortest path in an unweighted graph, and DFS is used to find *a* path. This compiles, runs, and returns a wrong answer only when a genuinely shorter path exists that DFS's neighbor-iteration order happened to explore later — meaning it's a bug that survives testing on any graph where DFS's first discovery happens to also be shortest, and only surfaces on a graph shaped adversarially against it.

The fix is not to make DFS smarter — it's to recognize the word "shortest" (or "minimum number of steps," "fewest moves") in unweighted-graph problems as a hard signal for BFS, full stop.

Recursive DFS pushes one stack frame per node on the current path, so on a long chain (a linked-list-shaped graph, or a deeply nested tree) the recursion depth equals the chain length. Many languages cap recursion depth well below what a large real-world graph can produce — Python's default limit is 1000, hit trivially by a graph with a few thousand sequentially-chained nodes.

The fix, when the graph might be deep, is the iterative DFS from the code slide above — it uses an explicit stack on the heap instead of the call stack, which is bounded only by available memory rather than a language-imposed recursion limit.

slides.sectionTitle: Marking visited on enqueue, not dequeue
slides.markdown:
In BFS, marking a node visited when it's **dequeued** instead of when it's **enqueued** looks harmless but silently breaks correctness on any graph where a node can be reached via more than one path. The same node can end up enqueued multiple times (once per incoming edge discovered before it's processed), wasting work and, in some formulations (e.g. counting distinct "discoveries"), producing an outright wrong answer.

The rule that avoids this: mark a node visited the instant you decide to enqueue it, not when you eventually process it. That's the single line most BFS bugs trace back to.
